5.1.summary:
When getting out of bed feels hard, remind yourself what you're getting up for: to do the work of a human being. Plants, birds, ants and bees all get on with their part in the world. Marcus is arguing with himself here, and his lazier side keeps answering back: but it's nicer under the covers, but I need rest.

Rest matters, he concedes, but nature puts limits on it, just as it does on food, and we overshoot those limits while stopping short on effort. People who love a craft forget to eat for it. If you cared about being a good person as much as a dancer cares about dancing, you wouldn't be dragging your feet over work that serves others.
5.1.today: Think of the snooze button pressed for the third time, or the dread of Monday that has nothing to do with the work itself. Compare it with how easily you lose whole evenings to a hobby you love, practising chords or tinkering with a bike, without once checking the time.

5.2.summary: You can drop a troubling or unhelpful thought almost as soon as it arrives, and with it, find calm straight away. Marcus says this is easy, which is partly encouragement to himself. The point is that a disturbing impression only takes hold if you keep it and add to it.

5.3.summary:
If something is right to do or say, do it, and don't let criticism put you off. Other people's comments come from their own minds and impulses, which are theirs to manage, not yours.

Keep going straight ahead, following your own nature and the nature of the whole, meaning the way the universe works and your part in it. For Marcus these two paths are really one: what's good for you as a reasonable, sociable being is what fits the world.
5.3.today: Speaking up in a meeting when something isn't right, or choosing to cycle to work while friends tease you about it. If you're confident it's the right thing, the eye-rolls and the sarcastic comment in the group chat are theirs to deal with.

5.4.summary:
Marcus pictures his life as a steady walk through what nature brings, ending when he falls and rests. At death he will breathe back into the air he draws in daily and return to the earth.

That earth gave his parents what made him, his nurse the milk that fed him, and him food for years. It carries him even as he misuses it. Death here is a return, not a loss, and the tone is gratitude rather than dread.

5.5.summary:
You may not be especially clever, Marcus tells himself, but most of what makes a good person has nothing to do with talent. Sincerity, seriousness, hard work, contentment with little, kindness, frankness, not getting caught up in trivia: these are all within your power right now.

So there's no excuse for grumbling, flattering, showing off, whining about your health or fretting to please people. Nothing in your nature forces you into those habits. And if you really are a bit slow, the answer is to work at it, not to wallow in it.
5.5.today: It's easy to say you're just not a people person, or not organised by nature. But turning up on time, giving a straight answer, not moaning in the staff kitchen and not angling for compliments on your post need no special gift.

5.6.summary:
There are three ways of doing someone a favour. One person keeps a tally and reminds you of it. Another says nothing but privately counts you as in their debt. The third barely notices what they've done, like a vine that produces grapes and then simply gets on with producing more next season.

Marcus wants to be the third kind. An imagined critic objects that social creatures should be aware of the good they do. Marcus answers that this misses the point: doing good without keeping score won't make you careless about others. It makes kindness ordinary, the natural thing you do.
5.6.today: Think of the friend who helps you move house and never mentions it again, compared with the one who brings it up whenever they need something. Or the colleague who covers your shift and doesn't need it noted on the team channel.

5.7.summary: Marcus quotes an old Athenian prayer asking Zeus simply for rain on their fields. Either we shouldn't pray at all, he says, or we should pray like this: plainly, for something shared and useful, not with elaborate bargaining or selfish requests.

5.8.summary:
When a doctor prescribes cold baths or walking barefoot, we accept it because it's for our health. Marcus uses Asclepius, the Greek god of healing, as his doctor. Illness, injury and loss can be seen the same way, as things the universe has prescribed. They fit your life the way squared stones fit together in a wall.

He gives two reasons to accept them. They were woven into your story from the start. And each one plays a part in keeping the whole universe healthy and running. Resenting what happens is, in a small way, trying to cut yourself out of that whole. It's a hard teaching and he doesn't soften it: even unpleasant things are to be welcomed.

5.9.summary:
Don't get disheartened when you fall short of your principles. Come back, be glad if most of what you do is decent, and love the life you're returning to. Treat philosophy not as a strict teacher you dread but as a soothing remedy, like a cool compress for sore eyes.

When you're tempted to think that some indulgence is more pleasant, notice that this is exactly how pleasure fools us. Generosity, freedom, simplicity, calm and reverence are more pleasant still, and nothing is more satisfying than understanding.
5.9.today: Missing a week of the gym, snapping at your kids, or breaking a promise to yourself about screen time. The habit isn't ruined. You simply pick it back up, without the self-punishment, and notice that most days you're doing all right.

5.10.summary:
Even philosophers find the world hard to understand, and our opinions keep shifting. Look at the things people chase and they're fleeting and cheap, the sort of thing a crook can own as easily as anyone. Look at the people around you and even the nicest are hard to bear, never mind yourself.

In all this murk and constant change, Marcus can't see anything worth grasping at. What remains is to stay patient until death and hold on to two thoughts: nothing will happen to you that doesn't fit how the universe works, and no one can make you act against your conscience. This is one of his bleaker moods, and he leaves it unsoftened.

5.11.summary: Keep asking yourself what you're using your mind for right now. What sort of person is running the show at this moment: a child, a hothead, a tyrant, a pet, a wild animal? The question is meant to catch you in the act, before the mood decides for you. His list also includes "a feeble woman", which reflects the prejudices of his time.
5.11.today: Mid-argument with a sibling, or halfway through an angry reply to a stranger online, ask who's typing. It might be a sulking teenager or a bully. The question alone can be enough to change course.

5.12.summary:
You can tell what's truly good by a simple test. If someone mocked wisdom, fairness, self-control or courage, you'd find it jarring. But if a comic playwright jokes that a rich man has so much stuff he hasn't room to relieve himself, everyone laughs and agrees.

That difference shows even ordinary people sense that wealth and luxury aren't really good. Marcus asks whether we should prize the very things a joke like that fits so neatly.
5.12.today: Jokes about people with garages full of unopened parcels or houses too packed with gadgets to move around land easily. Nobody makes the same joke about having too much honesty or patience.

5.13.summary: You are made of form and matter, and neither came from nothing nor will vanish into nothing. When you die, your parts will turn into other parts of the universe, and those into others again, endlessly. You yourself came about through that same process of change, as did your parents before you. Marcus adds that this holds even if the universe runs in repeating cycles, as some Stoics believed.

5.14.summary: Reason, and philosophy as the practice of it, needs nothing outside itself. It starts from its own principles and moves towards its own goal. That's why the Stoics called good actions by a Greek word meaning "right acts", actions that take the straight road. What makes an action good is the reasoning behind it, not how things turn out.

5.15.summary:
Things that don't belong to us as human beings, such as wealth, status and comfort, aren't part of what a human life is for. Our nature doesn't demand or promise them, and they don't help us towards our real aim, so they aren't good.

The proof is that we admire people who do without them. If those things were truly good, giving them up would make you worse, not better. Yet the more calmly someone goes without, the better we think of them.

5.16.summary:
Your mind takes on the colour of what you usually think about, the way cloth takes on dye. So soak it in good thoughts. One is that you can live well wherever you have to live, even in a palace, which for Marcus was not a fantasy but his daily life.

Another is that everything is made for a purpose and finds its good in that purpose. For beings who can reason, that purpose is living with and for others. The higher kinds of life, he argues, are the ones that reason, and reasoning creatures are made for each other.
5.16.today: What you scroll through on the train, the podcasts you play and the grumbles you repeat to yourself all shape the person you're becoming. Someone who rehearses grievances all day will find it hard to be cheerful at dinner.

5.17.summary: It's madness to want the impossible, and it's impossible for bad people not to behave badly. Expecting otherwise only sets you up to be upset. Marcus isn't excusing wrongdoing, just refusing to be surprised by it.

5.18.summary: Nothing happens to you that you aren't built to cope with. Others go through the same thing and stay steady, sometimes because they don't fully grasp what's happened, sometimes because they want to look brave. It would be shameful if ignorance or vanity proved stronger than wisdom.
5.18.today: You might see a friend shrug off a redundancy or a breakup partly to save face on social media. If pride can do that much, a clear understanding of what really matters can do at least as much for you.

5.19.summary: Events can't get inside your mind. They have no way in and no power to move it. Your mind moves itself, and what things seem like to you depends on the judgements it chooses to make about them. That's why the same event can leave one person shaken and another steady.

5.20.summary:
In one way, other people are your closest concern: you're meant to do them good and put up with them. But when someone blocks you from doing right, they become, in that respect, no different from weather or a wild animal, something outside you that isn't good or bad in itself.

They can get in the way of what you do, but not of how you think or what you intend. The mind can adapt and turn an obstacle into a chance to act well, so the thing in the road becomes part of the road.
5.20.today: A colleague who blocks your project might push you to find a better way through, or to practise patience you didn't know you had. A cancelled train becomes the hour you finally ring your grandmother.

5.21.summary: Revere the best thing in the universe, the reason that orders and uses everything. Then revere the best thing in yourself, which is the same kind of thing: your own reason, which uses everything else in you and steers your life. Marcus sees your mind as a small share of the mind behind the whole.

5.22.summary: Here's a test for whether you've really been harmed: if the community isn't harmed, neither are you. And if it is harmed, anger at the person who did it is still the wrong response. Show them where they went wrong instead.
5.22.today: Someone parks badly or takes the last biscuit in the office: no one is really harmed. If a neighbour dumps rubbish on the shared green, have a calm word with them rather than writing a furious post in the local group.

5.23.summary:
Keep reminding yourself how fast everything passes. Matter flows like a river, actions keep changing, causes vary endlessly and almost nothing stands still. Behind and ahead of you is a bottomless stretch of past and future in which everything disappears.

So it's foolish to get puffed up about things, or tormented by them, as though they were permanent. Whatever troubles you will only trouble you for a short while.

5.24.summary: Picture all the matter in the universe and your tiny share of it, all of time and your brief moment, everything fate sets in motion and your small part in it. The point is to see your worries at their true size.

5.25.summary: If someone wrongs me, that's their business: their character and their actions belong to them. My business is to accept what the universe has given me right now and do what my own nature asks of me right now. Marcus keeps the two firmly separate.
5.25.today: When a friend lets you down or someone is rude to you at the till, their behaviour is theirs to answer for. Yours is how you respond and what you do next with your afternoon.

5.26.summary:
Your mind, the part that thinks and decides, should stay calm whatever the body feels, pleasure or pain. Keep those feelings in their place rather than letting them take charge.

Marcus is realistic: body and mind are one system, so sensations will reach the mind and you shouldn't pretend they don't. What you can refuse to do is add the judgement that this pain is a disaster or this pleasure is a great good.
5.26.today: A toothache or a sleepless night will register, and pretending otherwise is pointless. The extra step to avoid is the story that comes after it: the day is ruined, I can't cope. Likewise you can enjoy cake without deciding you can't be happy without it.

5.27.summary: To live with the gods means showing, by how you live, that you're content with what you've been given and that you follow the spirit within you, your inner reason and conscience. Marcus believes Zeus gave every person this as a guide, a piece of the divine. In everyday terms, it's your own capacity to think clearly and act rightly.

5.28.summary:
Getting angry at someone because their breath or armpits smell achieves nothing. That's just how they are. You might say they have reason and could work out that they're offending people. Well, so do you: use yours to help them see it. Tell them, kindly. If they listen, the problem is solved and anger never came into it.

The cryptic last line seems to mean: don't make a theatrical scene, and don't fawn over them either.
5.28.today: The modern version is the colleague who chews loudly or the flatmate who never empties the bin. Seething silently or complaining about them to others helps no one. A quiet, friendly word usually does.

5.29.summary:
You can live now as you would want to live at the end, free and true to yourself. If circumstances make that impossible, Marcus says, leave life without treating it as a disaster: the house is smoky, so I walk out. This reflects the ancient Stoic view that ending one's life could be acceptable when living well became impossible.

But as long as nothing drives him out, he stays, free, and nobody can stop him choosing to live as a reasonable, sociable person should.

5.30.summary: The mind behind the universe is sociable. It has arranged lower things to serve higher ones and fitted the higher ones, reasoning beings, to work together. Everything has its place and share. For Marcus, our urge to cooperate reflects how the whole is built.

5.31.summary:
Marcus takes stock. How has he treated the gods, his parents, brothers, children, teachers, nurses, friends, relatives and slaves? Could it be said of him that he never wronged anyone in word or deed?

Then he reminds himself of all he's been through and endured, that his story could be considered complete and his service done, and of the beauty he's seen, the pleasures and pains he's risen above, the honours he's turned down and the difficult people he's been kind to. It's an honest audit, and also a source of quiet strength.
5.31.today: At a birthday, the end of a job or late on a quiet evening, run through the people in your life: your parents, your children, your old teachers, the friend you lost touch with. Ask whether you've treated them well, and notice too how much you've already come through.

5.32.summary: Why should people who don't know what they're doing unsettle someone who does? And who really knows? Whoever understands how things begin and end, and the reason that runs through and governs the universe over time. Seeing the big picture keeps you steady among confused people.

5.33.summary:
Soon you'll be ashes or bones, a name or not even that, and a name is just a sound. What people prize in life is hollow and petty, like puppies snapping at each other or children laughing one moment and crying the next. Honesty and decency seem to have left the earth.

So why cling on, or care about reputation? Wait calmly for death, whether it ends you or moves you elsewhere. Until then, enough is honouring the gods, doing good to people, putting up with them and holding back. Everything beyond your own body and breath isn't yours and isn't in your control.
5.33.today: Think of the office squabble over who gets the window desk, or a feud in the comments over a football result. Seen from a distance they look a lot like children fighting over a toy and forgetting it ten minutes later.

5.34.summary: A life can flow smoothly and happily if you think and act on the right path. Two things belong to every reasoning being, gods and humans alike: no one else can block your mind, and your good lies in being fair and acting fairly. If you let your wanting rest there, you won't be disappointed.

5.35.summary: Before getting upset, ask two questions. Is this my own wrongdoing, or the result of it? Has the common good been harmed? If the answer to both is no, there's nothing to be troubled about. Most things that bother us fail both tests.

5.36.summary:
Don't get swept away by how things look. Help people as far as you can and as far as they need, but when they lose things that aren't truly good or bad, such as money or position, don't treat it as a real harm. That's a bad habit. Marcus offers the image of an old man asking for his foster-child's spinning top back, knowing all along it's only a toy: you can go along with someone's loss while seeing it clearly.

The ending is fragmentary. Someone shouting from a public platform forgets what such things are worth, and a man who says he lost his good fortune is told that real good fortune is a good character, good feelings and good actions.
5.36.today: When a friend is gutted about a dent in their car or a missed promotion, you can sympathise and help without agreeing that their life is ruined. Real good luck is being the kind of person who stays decent whatever happens to the car.
